claim: MECP2 mutations underlying Rett syndrome cause widespread misregulation of gene expression.
source: MECP2 mutations underlying Rett syndrome cause widespread misregulation of gene expression.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the citation context of the manuscript.

claim: In an ex vivo brain preparation from the pond turtle Trachemys scripta elegans, an intraexonic splicing event in the brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) gene generates a truncated mRNA transcript in naïve brain.
source: In an ex vivo brain preparation from the pond turtle Trachemys scripta elegans, an intraexonic splicing event in the brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) gene generates a truncated mRNA transcript in naïve brain that is suppressed upon classical conditioning.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including RT-PCR and sequencing results.

claim: The truncated BDNF mRNA transcript is suppressed upon classical conditioning.
source: In an ex vivo brain preparation from the pond turtle Trachemys scripta elegans, an intraexonic splicing event in the brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) gene generates a truncated mRNA transcript in naïve brain that is suppressed upon classical conditioning.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced tBDNF2a transcript levels after conditioning.

claim: MeCP2 and its partners, splicing factor Y-box binding protein 1 (YB-1) and methylcytosine dioxygenase 1 (Tet1), bind to BDNF chromatin in naïve preparations.
source: MeCP2 and its partners, splicing factor Y-box binding protein 1 (YB-1) and methylcytosine dioxygenase 1 (Tet1), bind to BDNF chromatin in naïve but dissociate during conditioning; the dissociation correlating with decreased DNA methylation.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing binding of these proteins to tBDNF in naïve preparations.

claim: MeCP2, YB-1, and Tet1 dissociate from BDNF chromatin during conditioning.
source: MeCP2 and its partners, splicing factor Y-box binding protein 1 (YB-1) and methylcytosine dioxygenase 1 (Tet1), bind to BDNF chromatin in naïve but dissociate during conditioning; the dissociation correlating with decreased DNA methylation.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing reduced binding after conditioning.

claim: The dissociation of MeCP2, YB-1, and Tet1 from BDNF chromatin correlates with decreased DNA methylation.
source: MeCP2 and its partners, splicing factor Y-box binding protein 1 (YB-1) and methylcytosine dioxygenase 1 (Tet1), bind to BDNF chromatin in naïve but dissociate during conditioning; the dissociation correlating with decreased DNA methylation.
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data showing demethylation during conditioning.

claim: Conditioning results in new occupancy of BDNF chromatin by DNA insulator protein CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF).
source: Surprisingly, conditioning results in new occupancy of BDNF chromatin by DNA insulator protein CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF), which is associated with suppression of splicing in conditioning.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data showing increased CTCF binding during conditioning.

claim: CTCF occupancy is associated with suppression of splicing in conditioning.
source: Surprisingly, conditioning results in new occupancy of BDNF chromatin by DNA insulator protein CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF), which is associated with suppression of splicing in conditioning.
evidence: This is supported by siRNA experiments showing that CTCF knockdown during conditioning restores splicing.

claim: Knockdown of MeCP2 is instrumental for splicing of tBDNF2a.
source: Knockdown of MeCP2 shows it is instrumental for splicing and inhibits Tet1 and CTCF binding thereby negatively impacting DNA methylation and conditioning-dependent splicing regulation.
evidence: This is supported by siRNA experiments showing reduced tBDNF2a transcript after MeCP2 knockdown.

claim: MeCP2 knockdown inhibits Tet1 binding to BDNF.
source: Knockdown of MeCP2 shows it is instrumental for splicing and inhibits Tet1 and CTCF binding thereby negatively impacting DNA methylation and conditioning-dependent splicing regulation.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data showing reduced Tet1 binding after MeCP2 siRNA treatment.

claim: MeCP2 knockdown inhibits CTCF binding to BDNF.
source: Knockdown of MeCP2 shows it is instrumental for splicing and inhibits Tet1 and CTCF binding thereby negatively impacting DNA methylation and conditioning-dependent splicing regulation.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data showing reduced CTCF binding after MeCP2 siRNA treatment.

claim: MeCP2 knockdown negatively impacts DNA methylation.
source: Knockdown of MeCP2 shows it is instrumental for splicing and inhibits Tet1 and CTCF binding thereby negatively impacting DNA methylation and conditioning-dependent splicing regulation.
evidence: This is supported by BSP data showing altered methylation patterns after MeCP2 siRNA treatment.

claim: MeCP2 knockdown negatively impacts conditioning-dependent splicing regulation.
source: Knockdown of MeCP2 shows it is instrumental for splicing and inhibits Tet1 and CTCF binding thereby negatively impacting DNA methylation and conditioning-dependent splicing regulation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that MeCP2 siRNA affects the normal conditioning-dependent suppression of splicing.

claim: Mutations in MECP2 can have secondary effects on DNA methylation and alternative splicing.
source: Thus, mutations in MECP2 can have secondary effects on DNA methylation and alternative splicing.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that MeCP2 knockdown affects Tet1 binding and DNA methylation patterns.

claim: Rett syndrome (RTT) is an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder caused by mutations in the methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2) gene.
source: Rett syndrome (RTT) is an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder caused by mutations in the methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2) gene (Amir et al., 1999; Bienvenu and Chelly, 2006; Lyst and Bird, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Loss of MeCP2 function in RTT leads to progressive neurological dysfunction including severe intellectual disabilities.
source: Loss of MeCP2 function in RTT leads to progressive neurological dysfunction including severe intellectual disabilities.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rett syndrome.

claim: MeCP2 binds to 5-methylcytosine (5mC) at CG and non-CG dinucleotides, particularly methylated CA.
source: MeCP2 binds to 5-methylcytosine (5mC) at CG and non-CG dinucleotides, particularly methylated CA, and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC; Mellén et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2015; Gabel et al., 2015; Kinde et al., 2015) across the genome.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MeCP2 binds to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) across the genome.
source: MeCP2 binds to 5-methylcytosine (5mC) at CG and non-CG dinucleotides, particularly methylated CA, and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC; Mellén et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2015; Gabel et al., 2015; Kinde et al., 2015) across the genome.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutations that give rise to RTT result in widespread misregulation of genes consistent with a role in transcriptional regulation.
source: Mutations that give rise to RTT result in widespread misregulation of genes consistent with a role in transcriptional regulation (Lyst and Bird, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: MeCP2 directly suppresses microRNA processing affecting dendritic growth and possibly neural development.
source: Recent evidence indicates that MeCP2 also directly suppresses microRNA processing affecting dendritic growth and possibly neural development (Cheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Alternative splicing of pre-mRNAs of active genes is ubiquitous in the eukaryotic genome.
source: Alternative splicing of pre-mRNAs of active genes is ubiquitous in the eukaryotic genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge in molecular biology.

claim: As many as 90% of genes are affected by alternative splicing.
source: It is estimated that as many as 90% of genes are affected by alternative splicing and its importance in brain has recently received a great deal of attention (Scheckel et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MeCP2 partners with the Y-box binding protein 1 (YB-1) that binds DNA or RNA and is involved in alternative splicing events.
source: With respect to MeCP2 function, Young et al. (2005) found that MeCP2 partners with the Y-box binding protein 1 (YB-1) that binds DNA or RNA and is involved in alternative splicing events (Matsumoto and Wolffe, 1998; Gonzales et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MeCP2 associates directly with other splice regulatory factors.
source: More recently, MeCP2 was found to associate directly with other splice regulatory factors and, importantly, mutations in MECP2 that occur in RTT disrupt these interactions (Long et al., 2011; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutations in MECP2 that occur in RTT disrupt interactions with splice regulatory factors.
source: More recently, MeCP2 was found to associate directly with other splice regulatory factors and, importantly, mutations in MECP2 that occur in RTT disrupt these interactions (Long et al., 2011; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Aberrant alternative splicing resulting from a loss of MeCP2 may be an important contributor in RTT.
source: These studies suggest that aberrant alternative splicing resulting from a loss of MeCP2 may be an important contributor in RTT.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited studies on MeCP2 and splicing factors.

claim: MeCP2 is a highly phosphorylated protein.
source: MeCP2 is a highly phosphorylated protein and mutations at phosphorylated sites cause RTT-like behaviors in mice (Ebert et al., 2013; Lyst et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutations at phosphorylated sites of MeCP2 cause RTT-like behaviors in mice.
source: MeCP2 is a highly phosphorylated protein and mutations at phosphorylated sites cause RTT-like behaviors in mice (Ebert et al., 2013; Lyst et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The BDNF gene is an established target of MeCP2 in turtle as it is in humans and rodents.
source: The BDNF gene is an established target of MeCP2 in turtle as it is in humans and rodents (Amir et al., 1999; Bambah-Mukku et al., 2014; Ambigapathy et al., 2015) and BDNF transcripts are alternatively spliced (Liu et al., 2005; Aid et al., 2007; Pruunsild et al., 2007; Ambigapathy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: BDNF transcripts are alternatively spliced.
source: The BDNF gene is an established target of MeCP2 in turtle as it is in humans and rodents (Amir et al., 1999; Bambah-Mukku et al., 2014; Ambigapathy et al., 2015) and BDNF transcripts are alternatively spliced (Liu et al., 2005; Aid et al., 2007; Pruunsild et al., 2007; Ambigapathy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Splicing of the BDNF gene in turtle (tBDNF) results in a 40 base pair (bp) deletion within the protein coding sequence that generates a novel truncated BDNF transcript (tBDNF2a) and protein.
source: We previously determined that splicing of the BDNF gene in turtle (tBDNF) results in a 40 base pair (bp) deletion within the protein coding sequence that generates a novel truncated BDNF transcript (tBDNF2a) and protein (Ambigapathy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The intraexonic splicing event in tBDNF is regulated by conditioning such that splicing occurs in the naïve, untrained state and is rapidly and completely suppressed during training.
source: Importantly, this intraexonic splicing event is regulated by conditioning such that splicing occurs in the naïve, untrained state and is rapidly and completely suppressed during training.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the authors' previous work.

claim: Suppression of tBDNF2a splicing is stimulus-specific.
source: Moreover, suppression is stimulus-specific. Splicing is inhibited by paired, but not unpaired, nerve stimulation and not by general increases in neuronal excitability evoked by application of glutamate or high potassium (Ambigapathy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Splicing of tBDNF2a is inhibited by paired, but not unpaired, nerve stimulation.
source: Moreover, suppression is stimulus-specific. Splicing is inhibited by paired, but not unpaired, nerve stimulation and not by general increases in neuronal excitability evoked by application of glutamate or high potassium (Ambigapathy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Splicing of tBDNF2a is not inhibited by general increases in neuronal excitability evoked by application of glutamate or high potassium.
source: Moreover, suppression is stimulus-specific. Splicing is inhibited by paired, but not unpaired, nerve stimulation and not by general increases in neuronal excitability evoked by application of glutamate or high potassium (Ambigapathy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: In naïve preparations, MeCP2 binds to methylated sites in DNA upstream of the tBDNF splice site to yield truncated tBDNF2a.
source: In naïve preparations, MeCP2 binds to methylated sites in DNA upstream of the tBDNF splice site to yield truncated tBDNF2a.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data presented in the manuscript.

claim: During conditioning, the tBDNF site undergoes dynamic loss of 5mC and 5hmC.
source: During conditioning, the site undergoes dynamic loss of 5mC and 5hmC, MeCP2 dissociates, and tBDNF2a splicing is suppressed.
evidence: This is supported by BSP and MeDIP data presented in the manuscript.

claim: During conditioning, MeCP2 dissociates from the tBDNF site and tBDNF2a splicing is suppressed.
source: During conditioning, the site undergoes dynamic loss of 5mC and 5hmC, MeCP2 dissociates, and tBDNF2a splicing is suppressed.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP and RT-PCR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Knockdown of MeCP2, YB-1 or Tet1 inhibits splicing of tBDNF2a.
source: Furthermore, knockdown of MeCP2, YB-1 or Tet1 inhibits splicing of tBDNF2a.
evidence: This is supported by siRNA experiments and RT-PCR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Demethylation and loss of MeCP2 during conditioning are correlated with binding of the DNA insulator protein CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF).
source: Demethylation and loss of MeCP2 during conditioning are correlated with binding of the DNA insulator protein CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF), leading to the idea that CTCF suppresses splicing.
evidence: This is supported by BSP, ChIP, and correlation analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: CTCF suppresses splicing of tBDNF2a.
source: Demethylation and loss of MeCP2 during conditioning are correlated with binding of the DNA insulator protein CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF), leading to the idea that CTCF suppresses splicing.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation data and supported by CTCF siRNA experiments.

claim: MeCP2 loss of function generates unexpected secondary deficits in patterns of gene methylation.
source: These findings suggest a new perspective for understanding mechanisms underlying RTT; that MeCP2 loss of function generates unexpected secondary deficits in patterns of gene methylation that results both in aberrant binding by DNA regulatory proteins and in alternative splicing.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that MeCP2 knockdown affects Tet1 binding and methylation patterns.

claim: MeCP2 loss of function results in aberrant binding by DNA regulatory proteins.
source: These findings suggest a new perspective for understanding mechanisms underlying RTT; that MeCP2 loss of function generates unexpected secondary deficits in patterns of gene methylation that results both in aberrant binding by DNA regulatory proteins and in alternative splicing.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing altered CTCF and Tet1 binding after MeCP2 knockdown.

claim: MeCP2 loss of function results in aberrant alternative splicing.
source: These findings suggest a new perspective for understanding mechanisms underlying RTT; that MeCP2 loss of function generates unexpected secondary deficits in patterns of gene methylation that results both in aberrant binding by DNA regulatory proteins and in alternative splicing.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing altered splicing patterns after MeCP2 knockdown.

claim: The deficits caused by MeCP2 loss of function are exposed in a physiological learning-dependent context, conditioning, and not under steady state conditions.
source: Further, and importantly, we show that the deficits are exposed in a physiological learning-dependent context, conditioning, and not under steady state conditions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that MeCP2 siRNA effects are most pronounced during conditioning.

claim: The vertebrate BDNF gene consists of a number of unique non-coding 5' exons each having its own promoter that regulates a common 3' protein coding exon with a variable 3' untranslated region (UTR).
source: The vertebrate BDNF gene consists of a number of unique non-coding 5' exons each having its own promoter that regulates a common 3' protein coding exon with a variable 3' untranslated region (UTR) that codes for expression of a preproBDNF precursor protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BDNF gene structure.

claim: The BDNF gene encodes two-part transcripts having one non-coding exon spliced to the common protein coding sequence.
source: Therefore, the BDNF gene encodes two-part transcripts having one non-coding exon spliced to the common protein coding sequence.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BDNF gene structure.

claim: After intracellular processing, proBDNF undergoes proteolytic conversion to form the mature BDNF protein involved in numerous cellular functions including cell growth, synapse formation and learning.
source: After intracellular processing, proBDNF undergoes proteolytic conversion to form the mature BDNF protein involved in numerous cellular functions including cell growth, synapse formation and learning (Lu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Three non-coding 5' exons (exons I-III) and their promoters and one 3' protein coding exon (exon IV) were identified for the tBDNF gene in turtle.
source: We previously identified three non-coding 5' exons (exons I-III) and their promoters and one 3' protein coding exon (exon IV) for the tBDNF gene in turtle (Ambigapathy et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Exon II generates four mRNA transcripts designated tBDNF2a-d each having a short, intermediate, or long 3'UTR.
source: Exon II generates four mRNA transcripts designated tBDNF2a-d each having a short, intermediate, or long 3'UTR (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The alternatively spliced tBDNF2a transcript encoding the truncated BDNF protein has an intermediate 3'UTR like tBDNF2c.
source: The alternatively spliced tBDNF2a transcript encoding the truncated BDNF protein has an intermediate 3'UTR like tBDNF2c (Figure 1A) but is generated by an intraexonic splicing event in coding exon IV that removes 40 bp (13 amino acids) out of the distal sequence (Figure 1B) that we described previously in relation to conditioning (Ambigapathy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and illustrated in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: The 40 bp deletion in tBDNF2a produces a frame shift resulting in an early stop codon and unique C-terminal end.
source: This deletion produces a frame shift resulting in an early stop codon and unique C-terminal end (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: PCR of naïve samples using genomic DNA as template showed a single band at 225 bp.
source: The results from PCR of naïve samples showed a single band from genomic DNA at 225 bp (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PCR using cDNA as a template produced two bands, one at 225 bp and a band that is 40 bp smaller at 185 bp.
source: By comparison, using cDNA as a template, two bands were obtained, one at 225 bp and a band that is 40 bp smaller at 185 bp.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Sequencing verified that the larger PCR band from cDNA is from the tBDNF2b-d transcripts and the smaller band is tBDNF2a.
source: Sequencing verified that the larger band is from the tBDNF2b-d transcripts which are identical in this region of the coding sequence and the smaller band is tBDNF2a generated from the atypical 40 bp deletion (Figure 1C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data.

claim: All four tBDNF exon II transcripts are expressed in naïve, untrained preparations.
source: All four tBDNF exon II transcripts are expressed in naïve, untrained preparations (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: After 15 min of conditioning all of the tBDNF exon II transcripts are significantly downregulated.
source: However, after 15 min of conditioning all of the transcripts are significantly downregulated (Figure 1D,C15) as was reported previously (Ambigapathy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D and citation to previous work.

claim: The tBDNF2a transcript is nearly completely suppressed to just 8% of naïve values after conditioning.
source: The tBDNF2a transcript, specifically, is nearly completely suppressed to just 8% of naïve values after conditioning which is shown quantitatively in Figure 1E (n = 5/group, p=0.001, N vs. C15 min).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The MeCP2 siRNA resulted in knockdown of total MeCP2 protein expression to an average of 59% of normal naïve levels.
source: The siRNA resulted in knockdown of total MeCP2 protein expression to an average of 59% of normal naïve levels (Figure 1F, n = 4/group, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Bath application of the MeCP2 siRNA to naïve preparations resulted in substantial inhibition of the tBDNF2a transcript to about 40% of naïve values.
source: Significantly, bath application of the MeCP2 siRNA to naïve preparations resulted in substantial inhibition of the tBDNF2a transcript as shown in Figure 1D (arrow) that was on average about 40% of naïve values (Figure 1E, p=0.001, N vs. MeCP2 siRNA).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: A scrambled negative control siRNA showed no reduction in expression of the spliced tBDNF2a transcript compared to normal naïve.
source: A scrambled negative control siRNA (Silencer #1, Ambion) showed no reduction in expression of the spliced tBDNF2a transcript compared to normal naïve (Figure 1D–E, n = 2).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: The other tBDNF transcripts, 2b-d, were not inhibited by application of the MeCP2 siRNA.
source: Importantly, the other tBDNF transcripts, 2b-d, were not inhibited by application of the MeCP2 siRNA (Figure 1G; n = 5/group, p<0.05, N vs. tBDNF2c; p=0.43, N vs. 2b and 2d) showing that it was selective in reducing tBDNF2a.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In naïve preparations, nearly all of the CG sites in the tBDNF coding sequence are methylated.
source: In naïve preparations, nearly all of the CG sites are methylated (Figure 2A, middle panel).
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: After only 15 min of conditioning, CG sites in the tBDNF coding sequence undergo active demethylation.
source: After only 15 min of conditioning, they undergo active demethylation (F(1,82) = 63.8, p<0.0001, N vs. C15 min) that does not occur following pseudoconditioning trials of randomly unpaired stimuli (F(1,82) = 0.15, p=0.70, N vs. Ps).
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Demethylation of CG sites does not occur following pseudoconditioning trials of randomly unpaired stimuli.
source: After only 15 min of conditioning, they undergo active demethylation (F(1,82) = 63.8, p<0.0001, N vs. C15 min) that does not occur following pseudoconditioning trials of randomly unpaired stimuli (F(1,82) = 0.15, p=0.70, N vs. Ps).
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Selected CA sites in the tBDNF coding sequence are either methylated in naïve and demethylated after conditioning or methylated after conditioning.
source: We also observed that there are selected CA sites in the coding sequence that are either methylated in naïve and demethylated after conditioning (e.g., site 26, p=0.002) or methylated after conditioning (Figure 2A, lower panel, e.g., sites 27, 39, 40, 46, p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CA sites in the tBDNF coding region undergo active conditioning-dependent methylation/demethylation in only 15 min.
source: Therefore, in addition to CG dinucleotides, CA sites in the coding region also undergo active conditioning-dependent methylation/demethylation in only 15 min.
evidence: This is inferred from the bisulfite sequencing data showing changes in CA methylation.

claim: Splicing of the tBDNF2a transcript was significantly inhibited after zebularine or RG108 application compared to naïve and pseudoconditioned preparations.
source: Splicing of the tBDNF2a transcript was significantly inhibited after zebularine or RG108 application compared to naïve and pseudoconditioned preparations (Fig. 2B, F(3,16) = 80.0, n = 5/group, p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Demethylation has a causative role in cessation of splicing of the tBDNF2a transcript.
source: These data indicate a strong mechanistic role for demethylation in the cessation of splicing.
evidence: This is inferred from the DNMT inhibitor experiments showing that induced demethylation suppresses splicing.

claim: ChIP-qPCR showed strong binding of total MeCP2 protein to tBDNF in the naïve state corresponding with splicing of the tBDNF2a transcript.
source: ChIP-qPCR showed strong binding of total MeCP2 protein to tBDNF in the naïve state corresponding with splicing of the tBDNF2a transcript (Figure 2C, 2aON).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MeCP2 binding to tBDNF was observed in the region surveyed by primer set P1 which is upstream of the actual splice site.
source: This was observed in the region surveyed by primer set P1 which is, interestingly, upstream of the actual splice site.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data using primer set P1.

claim: With conditioning when the coding sequence undergoes rapid demethylation, ChIP indicates a significant reduction in MeCP2 binding to just 4% of naïve.
source: With conditioning when the coding sequence undergoes rapid demethylation, ChIP indicates a significant reduction in MeCP2 binding to just 4% of naïve (Figure 2C, n = 5/group, p<0.0001, N vs. C15 min) that corresponds with cessation of splicing and suppression of the tBDNF2a transcript (2aOFF).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: During conditioning, MeCP2 was observed to increase binding in the region surveyed by primer set P2.
source: During this time, MeCP2 was also observed to increase binding in the region surveyed by primer set P2 (Figure 2C, p=0.07) suggesting that it may be translocated to this downstream site rather than vacating genomic DNA entirely.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Levels of total MeCP2 protein were unchanged during conditioning.
source: These alterations in binding occurred even though levels of total MeCP2 protein were unchanged during conditioning (Figure 2D; n = 4/group, p=0.50).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: MeCP2 binding to tBDNF was significantly reduced in naïve preparations exposed to MeCP2 siRNA to 35% of normal naïve levels.
source: Finally, ChIP-qPCR verified that MeCP2 binding was significantly reduced in naïve preparations exposed to MeCP2 siRNA to 35% of normal naïve levels (Figure 2C, p<0.001, N vs. siRNA) corresponding well with the 40% reduction in the tBDNF2a transcript after MeCP2 siRNA (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The tBDNF protein coding sequence is rapidly demethylated during conditioning resulting in reduced MeCP2 binding upstream of the splice site that corresponds with suppression of the alternatively spliced truncated tBDNF2a transcript.
source: These findings indicate that the tBDNF protein coding sequence is rapidly demethylated during conditioning resulting in reduced MeCP2 binding upstream of the splice site that corresponds with suppression of the alternatively spliced truncated tBDNF2a transcript.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined BSP, ChIP, and RT-PCR data.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitations show a strong interaction of total MeCP2 protein with YB-1 in both naïve and conditioned preparations that was not altered by conditioning.
source: The results show a strong interaction of total MeCP2 protein with YB-1 in both naïve and conditioned preparations that was not altered by conditioning (Figure 3A, n = 3/group, p=0.91).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The MeCP2-YB-1 association requires the presence of RNA.
source: Additionally, we confirmed that the MeCP2-YB-1 association required the presence of RNA. Treatment of samples with DNaseI did not affect the co-IPs whereas treatment with RNase A inhibited it (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data with DNase and RNase treatment shown in Figure 3B.

claim: YB-1 was bound to the tBDNF coding region surveyed by primer set P1 in naïve preparations and was significantly reduced after conditioning.
source: Like MeCP2, ChIP indicated that YB-1 was bound to this region in naïve preparations and was significantly reduced after conditioning (Figure 3C, n = 5/group, p=0.02).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The overall level of YB-1 protein was not altered after 15 min of conditioning compared to naive.
source: Importantly, western blot data showed that the overall level of YB-1 protein was not altered after 15 min of conditioning compared to naive (n = 3/group, p=0.82).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data.

claim: YB-1 binds to the same region of the coding sequence as MeCP2 during splicing and is similarly released in conditioning when it is suppressed.
source: These results indicate that YB-1 binds to the same region of the coding sequence as MeCP2 during splicing and is similarly released in conditioning when it is suppressed.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP data showing parallel binding patterns for MeCP2 and YB-1.

claim: Tet1 is bound to the tBDNF coding sequence in naïve and dissociates after conditioning.
source: ChIP-qPCR showed that Tet1 is bound to the coding sequence in naïve and dissociates after conditioning (Figure 3C, p<0.001, N vs. C15 min).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MeCP2, YB-1 and Tet1 are bound to a region upstream of the splice site in naïve preparations during splicing of the truncated tBDNF2a transcript and all three dissociate during conditioning when splicing stops.
source: Taken together, the ChIP data show that MeCP2, YB-1 and Tet1 are bound to a region upstream of the splice site in naïve preparations during splicing of the truncated tBDNF2a transcript and all three dissociate during conditioning when splicing stops.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined ChIP data for all three proteins.

claim: Release of MeCP2, YB-1, and Tet1 binding during conditioning corresponds with significantly increased levels of H3K4me3 in the same region of the coding sequence.
source: Interestingly, release of binding during conditioning corresponds with changes in histone modifications in the same region of the coding sequence that consists of significantly increased levels of H3K4me3 (Figure 3C, p=0.01) and reduced H3K27me3 (p<0.01, N vs. C15 min), alterations that would lead to a more permissive, or open, chromatin structure.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Release of MeCP2, YB-1, and Tet1 binding during conditioning corresponds with reduced H3K27me3 in the same region of the coding sequence.
source: Interestingly, release of binding during conditioning corresponds with changes in histone modifications in the same region of the coding sequence that consists of significantly increased levels of H3K4me3 (Figure 3C, p=0.01) and reduced H3K27me3 (p<0.01, N vs. C15 min), alterations that would lead to a more permissive, or open, chromatin structure.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Bath application of YB-1 siRNA to naïve preparations resulted in a significant 53% knockdown of YB-1 protein expression compared to normal naïve.
source: Bath application of the siRNA to naïve preparations resulted in a significant 53% knockdown of YB-1 protein expression compared to normal naïve (Figure 3D, n = 3/group, p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Analysis of mRNA transcripts in naïve preparations treated with YB-1 siRNA showed that expression of spliced tBDNF2a was reduced to 42% of its normal naïve values.
source: Significantly, analysis of mRNA transcripts in naïve preparations treated with YB-1 siRNA showed that expression of spliced tBDNF2a was reduced to 42% of its normal naïve values (Figure 3E, n = 5/group; p=0.001).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Expression of the other three exon II transcripts (tBDNF2b-d) were not significantly affected by YB-1 siRNA treatment.
source: These findings were specific to the 2a transcript as expression of the other three exon II transcripts were not significantly affected by YB-1 siRNA treatment (tBDNF2b-d, F(1,28) = 0.10, p=0.75).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data.

claim: Tet1 siRNA applied to naïve nearly completely suppressed the tBDNF2a transcript to only 4% of normal naïve values.
source: These data are replotted here and show that Tet1 siRNA applied to naïve nearly completely suppressed the tBDNF2a transcript to only 4% of normal naïve values (Figure 3E, p=0.0003).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3E and cited from a previous study.

claim: YB-1 and Tet1 are key partners with MeCP2 that are required for alternative splicing of the tBDNF2a transcript.
source: Therefore, YB-1 and Tet1 are key partners with MeCP2 that are required for alternative splicing of the tBDNF2a transcript.
evidence: This is inferred from the siRNA experiments showing that knockdown of either YB-1 or Tet1 inhibits splicing.

claim: YB-1 ChIP was significantly inhibited from binding in naïve preparations treated with MeCP2 siRNA.
source: Assessment of YB-1 ChIP revealed that it was significantly inhibited from binding in naïve preparations treated with MeCP2 siRNA (Figure 3C, p=0.01, N vs. siRNA) as would be expected if MeCP2 recruits YB-1.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The MeCP2 siRNA did not alter the overall level of YB-1 protein compared to normal naïve.
source: Because MeCP2 also has a transcriptional function, control experiments were performed showing that the MeCP2 siRNA did not alter the overall level of YB-1 protein compared to normal naïve (n = 3/group, p=0.66).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data.

claim: Tet1 ChIP was significantly reduced by application of MeCP2 siRNA to naïve preparations.
source: Importantly, we also observed that Tet1 ChIP was significantly reduced by application of MeCP2 siRNA to naïve preparations (Figure 3C, p=0.02, N vs. siRNA).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Protein levels of Tet1 were unaffected by MeCP2 siRNA treatment.
source: This occurred even though protein levels of Tet1 were also unaffected by the treatment (n = 3/group, p=0.57).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data.

claim: The histone modifications H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 showed significantly reduced ChIP signals following MeCP2 siRNA treatment.
source: Further follow-up of these results indicated that the histone modifications analyzed here, H3K4me3 associated with active genes and H3K27me3 associated with repressed genes, showed significantly reduced ChIP signals following MeCP2 siRNA treatment (Figure 3C, H3K4me3, p=0.001; H3K27me3, p<0.01, N vs. siRNA) suggesting that MeCP2 also exerts control over chromatin structure.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MeCP2 exerts control over chromatin structure.
source: Further follow-up of these results indicated that the histone modifications analyzed here, H3K4me3 associated with active genes and H3K27me3 associated with repressed genes, showed significantly reduced ChIP signals following MeCP2 siRNA treatment (Figure 3C, H3K4me3, p=0.001; H3K27me3, p<0.01, N vs. siRNA) suggesting that MeCP2 also exerts control over chromatin structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the histone modification ChIP data after MeCP2 knockdown.

claim: Conditioning-induced demethylation was significantly inhibited following conditioning in MeCP2 siRNA as shown for individual CG sites in the coding sequence.
source: Our results further show that this was significantly inhibited following conditioning in MeCP2 siRNA as shown for individual CG sites in the coding sequence (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by BSP data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was an overall reduction in conditioning-induced demethylation across the coding sequence with MeCP2 siRNA treatment during conditioning compared to normal conditioning.
source: Grouped data show there was an overall reduction in conditioning-induced demethylation across the coding sequence with MeCP2 siRNA treatment during conditioning compared to normal conditioning (Figure 4B, left panel, p<0.0001, C15 min vs. C15 MeCP2 siRNA).
evidence: This is supported by BSP data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Inhibition of Tet1 tBDNF binding by MeCP2 siRNA treatment severely attenuates the demethylation process that normally takes place during conditioning.
source: Therefore, inhibition of Tet1 tBDNF binding by MeCP2 siRNA treatment severely attenuates the demethylation process that normally takes place during conditioning.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined ChIP and BSP data showing reduced Tet1 binding and reduced demethylation after MeCP2 siRNA.

claim: Levels of 5hmC were high in the tBDNF coding regions surveyed by primer sets P1 and P2 in naïve preparations.
source: Our results showed that levels of 5hmC were high in the coding regions surveyed by primer sets P1 and P2 in naïve preparations (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by MeDIP data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: After conditioning, values for 5hmC MeDIP were substantially reduced in all three primer set regions.
source: After conditioning, values for 5hmC MeDIP were substantially reduced in all three primer set regions (Figure 4D, n = 5/group, F(5,29) = 58.2, p=0.001, N vs. C15 min), presumably reflecting conversion by Tet-mediated iterative oxidation to unmethylated C (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by MeDIP data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Treatment of naïve preparations with MeCP2 siRNA that inhibited Tet1 tBDNF binding resulted in a significant reduction in 5hmC.
source: Moreover, treatment of naïve preparations with MeCP2 siRNA that inhibited Tet1 tBDNF binding also resulted in a significant reduction in 5hmC (Fig. 4D, F(5,29) = 33.4, p=0.001, N vs. N MeCP2 siRNA) consistent with Tet1's role in establishing this epigenetic mark.
evidence: This is supported by MeDIP data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In conditions in which Tet1 function is compromised by MeCP2 siRNA, 5mC predominates in the naïve state in place of 5hmC.
source: These findings suggest that in conditions in which Tet1 function is compromised by MeCP2 siRNA, 5mC predominates in the naïve state in place of 5hmC (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined MeDIP and BSP data.

claim: Analysis of the methylation status of the coding sequence after Tet1 siRNA application by BSP showed that it remained highly methylated similar to untreated naïve preparations.
source: Analysis of the methylation status of the coding sequence after Tet1 siRNA application by BSP showed that it remained highly methylated similar to untreated naïve preparations (Figure 5A, p=0.17).
evidence: This is supported by BSP data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Levels of 5hmC were nearly doubled after Tet1 siRNA treatment compared to normal naïve.
source: Further analysis by MeDIP demonstrated that levels of 5hmC were nearly doubled after Tet1 siRNA treatment compared to normal naïve (Figure 5B, p=0.001).
evidence: This is supported by MeDIP data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Binding of MeCP2 and YB-1 to the tBDNF coding sequence was significantly inhibited after Tet1 siRNA treatment.
source: Surprisingly, binding of MeCP2 and YB-1 to the tBDNF coding sequence was significantly inhibited (Figure 5C, n = 5/group, MeCP2, p<0.01, YB-1, p<0.01), which accounts for the suppression of splicing in Tet1 siRNA treated naïve preparations.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Tet3 binding to tBDNF was greatly increased after Tet1 siRNA treatment.
source: These data showed minimal binding in normal naïve preparations that was greatly increased after Tet1 siRNA treatment (Figure 5C, n = 3/group, p=0.001).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The enhanced binding of Tet3 after Tet1 siRNA was not accompanied by any changes in protein expression.
source: The enhanced binding of Tet3 was not accompanied by any changes in protein expression (Ambigapathy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The MeCP2-YB-1 complex was not recruited to methylated DNA under conditions in which there is loss of Tet1, which is replaced by Tet3.
source: These ChIP data indicate that the MeCP2-YB-1 complex was not recruited to methylated DNA under conditions in which there is loss of Tet1, which is replaced by Tet3.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP data showing reduced MeCP2-YB-1 binding and increased Tet3 binding after Tet1 siRNA.

claim: CTCF binding is modified by DNA methylation such that it is evicted by 5mC to control exon splicing in the lymphocyte CD45 model gene.
source: CTCF binding is also modified by DNA methylation such that it is evicted by 5mC to control exon splicing in the lymphocyte CD45 model gene (Shukla et al., 2011; Marina et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Expression of the CTCF protein was significantly increased to 168% over naïve values during conditioning.
source: Expression of the CTCF protein was observed to be regulated during conditioning as it was significantly increased to 168% over naïve values (Figure 6B, n = 5/group, p=0.001).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The CTCF siRNA resulted in a reduction in protein expression to 27% of normal naïve preparations.
source: The siRNA was designed against conserved CTCF sequences in the turtle (nt 1187–1212) that resulted in a reduction in protein expression to 27% of normal naïve preparations (Figure 6C, lower left panel, n = 3/group, p=0.001).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Application of CTCF siRNA to naïve preparations failed to have any effect on tBDNF2a splicing.
source: Application of the siRNA to naïve preparations failed to have any effect on tBDNF2a splicing, as shown by the semi-quantitative data (Figure 6C, lower right panel, n = 5/group, p=0.91, N vs. N CTCF siRNA).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: When conditioned preparations that normally suppress splicing were treated with CTCF siRNA, the tBDNF2a transcript was unmasked and splicing resumed at levels similar to normal naïve preparations.
source: Interestingly, however, when conditioned preparations that normally suppress splicing were treated with CTCF siRNA, the tBDNF2a transcript was unmasked and splicing resumed at levels similar to normal naïve preparations (Figure 6C, p<0.0001, C15 vs. C15 CTCF siRNA).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: CTCF insulates DNA sequences from the splicing apparatus during normal conditioning thereby suppressing the truncated tBDNF2a transcript.
source: These data provide compelling evidence that CTCF insulates DNA sequences from the splicing apparatus during normal conditioning thereby suppressing the truncated tBDNF2a transcript.
evidence: This is inferred from the CTCF siRNA experiments showing that CTCF knockdown during conditioning restores splicing.

claim: ChIP assays of CTCF binding to the coding region showed significantly increased signals within primer sets P1 and P3 during conditioning.
source: To provide additional support for our interpretation of splicing insulation, ChIP assays of CTCF binding to the coding region showed significantly increased signals within primer sets P1 and P3 during conditioning (Figure 6D, n = 5/group; P1: p=0.002; P3, p<0.05, N vs. C15 min).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There was strong CTCF binding to region P2 that was not conditioning-dependent.
source: While there was strong binding to region P2 this was not conditioning-dependent (Figure 6D, p=0.12).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Analysis with ChIP for RNAPIISer2 showed no significant conditioning-related changes in binding to the coding exon.
source: Analysis with ChIP for RNAPIISer2 showed no significant conditioning-related changes in binding to the coding exon (Figure 6E, n = 5/group; F(5,24) = 1.40, p=0.26) suggesting that CTCF does not affect binding of the elongating form of RNAPII.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: CTCF does not affect binding of the elongating form of RNAPII.
source: Analysis with ChIP for RNAPIISer2 showed no significant conditioning-related changes in binding to the coding exon (Figure 6E, n = 5/group; F(5,24) = 1.40, p=0.26) suggesting that CTCF does not affect binding of the elongating form of RNAPII.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAPIISer2 ChIP data showing no changes during conditioning.

claim: Depletion of MeCP2 by siRNA results in a significant reduction in CTCF ChIP of both naïve and conditioned preparations compared to untreated preparations.
source: The results showed a significant reduction in CTCF ChIP of both naïve and conditioned preparations treated by MeCP2 siRNA compared to untreated preparations (Figure 6D, N siRNA P1: p=0.01, C15 siRNA P1: p<0.0001; N siRNA P2: p<0.001, C15 siRNA P2: p<0.001) even though overall protein levels were unaffected by the treatment (Figure 6F, n = 3/group, p=0.44).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6D and western blot data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Overall CTCF protein levels were unaffected by MeCP2 siRNA treatment.
source: The results showed a significant reduction in CTCF ChIP of both naïve and conditioned preparations treated by MeCP2 siRNA compared to untreated preparations (Figure 6D, N siRNA P1: p=0.01, C15 siRNA P1: p<0.0001; N siRNA P2: p<0.001, C15 siRNA P2: p<0.001) even though overall protein levels were unaffected by the treatment (Figure 6F, n = 3/group, p=0.44).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The loss of Tet1 binding in MeCP2-treated preparations resulted in a functionally significant elevation in 5mC in the tBDNF coding sequence that would normally undergo conversion to unmethylated C during conditioning.
source: The loss of Tet1 binding in MeCP2-treated preparations resulted in a functionally significant elevation in 5mC in the tBDNF coding sequence that would normally undergo conversion to unmethylated C during conditioning.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined ChIP and BSP data showing reduced Tet1 binding and elevated methylation after MeCP2 siRNA.

claim: The change in methylation status after MeCP2 siRNA was accompanied by inhibition of CTCF binding during conditioning that can be attributed to its eviction by abnormally high levels of 5mC.
source: This change in methylation status was accompanied by inhibition of CTCF binding during conditioning that can be attributed, based on the work of others, to its eviction by abnormally high levels of 5mC.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined methylation and ChIP data, and supported by citations to previous work on CTCF and methylation.

claim: In MeCP2 null male mice, dynamically modified, but not stable, 5hmC loci were found to be significantly reduced compared to controls.
source: Interestingly, in MeCP2 null male mice, dynamically modified, but not stable, 5hmC loci were found to be significantly reduced compared to controls (Szulwach et al., 2011), consistent with our findings.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Depletion of MeCP2 protein may alter DNA methylation status indirectly by preventing binding of other DNA modifying proteins, including Tet.
source: Taken together, available evidence suggests that depletion of MeCP2 protein may alter DNA methylation status indirectly by preventing binding of other DNA modifying proteins, including Tet.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that MeCP2 knockdown reduces Tet1 binding and affects methylation patterns.

claim: MeCP2 and Tet1 are binding partners.
source: Evidence indicates that MeCP2 and Tet1 are binding partners (Cartron et al., 2013; Ambigapathy et al., 2015) but the functional impact of this relationship has been largely unstudied.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MeCP2 and Tet1 together may regulate the overall content of 5mC and 5hmC for dynamically modulated genes.
source: It is possible that MeCP2 and Tet1 together regulate the overall content of 5mC and 5hmC for dynamically modulated genes.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed interactions between MeCP2 and Tet1.

claim: Loss of MeCP2 destabilizes the regulatory process for control of DNA methylation across the genome.
source: Loss of MeCP2 destabilizes this regulatory process for control of DNA methylation across the genome.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing altered methylation patterns after MeCP2 knockdown.

claim: MeCP2 is a global regulator of chromatin structure and may serve as an integral component of the chromatin architecture itself.
source: An alternative but not mutually exclusive mechanism relates to the view that MeCP2 is a global regulator of chromatin structure and may serve as an integral component of the chromatin architecture itself (Skene et al., 2010; Cohen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Inhibition of MeCP2 severely depleted the tBDNF coding sequence of the histone modifications H3K4me3 and H3K27me3.
source: In our study, we observed that inhibition of MeCP2 severely depleted the tBDNF coding sequence of the histone modifications H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 that have a significant role in regulating gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data showing reduced histone modifications after MeCP2 siRNA.

claim: Loss of MeCP2 may affect learning-related tBDNF binding by regulatory proteins, including Tet1, through its action on controlling the accessibility of the surrounding chromatin structure.
source: Therefore, loss of MeCP2 may affect learning-related tBDNF binding by regulatory proteins, including Tet1, through its action on controlling the accessibility of the surrounding chromatin structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on histone modifications and protein binding after MeCP2 knockdown.

claim: Increased chromatin compaction observed in MeCP2-null neurons in vivo might restrict activity-dependent DNA regulatory mechanisms leading to a disruption in gene methylation and expression.
source: Along these lines, increased chromatin compaction observed in MeCP2-null neurons in vivo might restrict activity-dependent DNA regulatory mechanisms leading to a disruption in gene methylation and expression (Linhoff et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study and inferred from the current findings.

claim: The human BDNF gene codes for antisense BDNF transcripts that may additionally regulate transcript expression.
source: Notably, the human BDNF gene also codes for antisense BDNF transcripts that may additionally regulate transcript expression (Liu et al., 2005; Pruunsild et al., 2007) that may not be present in rat or mouse (Aid et al., 2007), although this is debatable (Modarresi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Internal splicing, although rare, has been documented in other genes from normal human and patient populations or rodents.
source: Although the intraexonic splicing event described here in turtle is an unconventional one, internal splicing, although rare, has been documented in other genes from normal human and patient populations (Cox et al., 2001; Tran et al., 2006; Madrigal et al., 2016) or rodents (Ye et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The truncated BDNF protein in turtle has a pattern of expression opposite to mature BDNF protein during conditioning.
source: While the functional significance of the spliced transcript in turtle BDNF is unknown, it generates a truncated protein that has a pattern of expression opposite to mature BDNF protein during conditioning (Ambigapathy et al., 2013), suggesting it may have a dominant negative function.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The truncated BDNF protein may have a dominant negative function.
source: While the functional significance of the spliced transcript in turtle BDNF is unknown, it generates a truncated protein that has a pattern of expression opposite to mature BDNF protein during conditioning (Ambigapathy et al., 2013), suggesting it may have a dominant negative function.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed expression pattern.

claim: Mechanisms regulating splicing, such as Tet-mediated DNA methylation and control of MeCP2-YB-1 and CTCF binding, are highly conserved and consistent with previous studies in mammals.
source: Our evidence indicates that mechanisms regulating splicing, such as Tet-mediated DNA methylation and control of MeCP2-YB-1 and CTCF binding, are highly conserved and consistent with previous studies in mammals (Young et al., 2005; Shukla et al., 2011; Maunakea et al., 2013; Marina et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citations to previous studies in mammals.

claim: A genome-wide analysis reported that gene body methylation and MeCP2 binding are enriched in alternatively spliced exons.
source: A genome-wide analysis reported that gene body methylation and MeCP2 binding are enriched in alternatively spliced exons and that inhibition of methylation disrupts selective targeting of MeCP2 resulting in aberrantly spliced transcripts (Maunakea et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Inhibition of methylation disrupts selective targeting of MeCP2 resulting in aberrantly spliced transcripts.
source: A genome-wide analysis reported that gene body methylation and MeCP2 binding are enriched in alternatively spliced exons and that inhibition of methylation disrupts selective targeting of MeCP2 resulting in aberrantly spliced transcripts (Maunakea et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: One proposed mechanism for MeCP2-mediated splicing is that MeCP2 recruits partner proteins that slow transcriptional elongation permitting more time for recognition of splice sites by the splicing machinery.
source: One proposed mechanism for MeCP2-mediated splicing is that MeCP2 recruits partner proteins that slow transcriptional elongation permitting more time for recognition of splice sites by the splicing machinery (Shukla et al., 2011; Luco et al., 2011; Maunakea et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MeCP2 partners directly with splice factors including YB-1 whose actions directly result in pre-mRNA alternative splicing.
source: MeCP2 partners directly with splice factors including YB-1 whose actions directly result in pre-mRNA alternative splicing (Young et al., 2005; Long et al., 2011; Gonzales et al., 2012; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DNA binding by MeCP2 has a central role in splicing and is regulated by DNA methylation status.
source: Therefore, accumulating evidence indicates that DNA binding by MeCP2 has a central role in splicing and is regulated by DNA methylation status.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature and the current experimental findings.

claim: The MeCP2 binding site (P1 region) is upstream from the splice site (P3 region).
source: Since the MeCP2 binding site (P1 region) is upstream from the splice site (P3 region), we propose that chromatin looping brings the two regions in close enough proximity to functionally interact.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data showing binding at different locations.

claim: Chromatin looping brings the MeCP2 binding site and the splice site in close enough proximity to functionally interact.
source: Since the MeCP2 binding site (P1 region) is upstream from the splice site (P3 region), we propose that chromatin looping brings the two regions in close enough proximity to functionally interact.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the spatial arrangement of binding sites.

claim: The downregulation of full-length tBDNF transcripts (2b-d) during conditioning is mediated by enhanced methylation of the exon II promoter and binding by the transcriptional repressor BHLHB2.
source: Instead, their conditioning-induced downregulation is mediated by enhanced methylation of the exon II promoter and binding by the transcriptional repressor BHLHB2 (Ambigapathy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The presence of high levels of 5hmC in naïve could explain why Tet1 ChIP shows strong binding even though DNA is methylated suggesting it may function to maintain the 5hmC mark.
source: The presence of high levels of 5hmC in naïve could explain why Tet1 ChIP shows strong binding even though DNA is methylated suggesting it may function to maintain the 5hmC mark (Hahn et al., 2013; Kinde et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the MeDIP and ChIP data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A reduction in 5hmC with MeCP2 knockdown is corroborated by Szulwach et al. (2011), but only for genomic loci in which 5hmC is dynamically regulated during development and not for those stably modified.
source: A reduction in 5hmC with MeCP2 knockdown is corroborated by Szulwach et al. (2011), but only for genomic loci in which 5hmC is dynamically regulated during development and not for those stably modified.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Stable 5hmC loci might have redundant mechanisms using multiple methyl-CpG-binding domain (MBD) proteins that negatively regulate genomic 5hmC content while dynamically regulated sites rely more heavily on MeCP2.
source: They argued that stable loci might have redundant mechanisms using multiple methyl-CpG-binding domain (MBD) proteins that negatively regulate genomic 5hmC content (and presumably Tet binding) while dynamically regulated sites rely more heavily on MeCP2.
evidence: This is an interpretation from a cited study.

claim: Application of Tet1 siRNA results in substantially increased levels of 5hmC, which has been observed by others using Tet1 knockdown in mammals.
source: Application of Tet1 siRNA, on the other hand, results in substantially increased levels of 5hmC, which has been observed by others using Tet1 knockdown in mammals (Feng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to a previous study.

claim: In conditions of Tet1 loss of function, DNA binding by MeCP2 was significantly reduced even though levels of methylation were high.
source: Moreover, and importantly, in conditions of Tet1 loss of function, DNA binding by MeCP2 was significantly reduced even though levels of methylation were high.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP and BSP data after Tet1 siRNA treatment.

claim: Inhibition of either MeCP2 or Tet1 negatively impacts the function of the other.
source: Therefore, inhibition of either MeCP2 or Tet1 negatively impacts the function of the other leading to the conclusion that, at least for splicing regulation of tBDNF, MeCP2 and Tet1 are critical functional partners.
evidence: This is inferred from the siRNA experiments showing reciprocal effects on binding.

claim: For splicing regulation of tBDNF, MeCP2 and Tet1 are critical functional partners.
source: Therefore, inhibition of either MeCP2 or Tet1 negatively impacts the function of the other leading to the conclusion that, at least for splicing regulation of tBDNF, MeCP2 and Tet1 are critical functional partners.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing their interdependent functions.

claim: Tet3 binds to tBDNF with loss of Tet1 and likely enhances the deposition of 5hmC that was observed.
source: Additionally, our data show that Tet3, which is expressed in substantial levels in turtle brain (Ambigapathy et al., 2015), binds to tBDNF with loss of Tet1 and likely enhances the deposition of 5hmC that was observed.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP and MeDIP data after Tet1 siRNA treatment.

claim: Preliminary findings show no MeCP2-Tet3 interaction.
source: While we confirmed our previous result that MeCP2-Tet1 co-IP in naïve preparations (Ambigapathy et al., 2015), preliminary findings show no MeCP2-Tet3 interaction (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on preliminary experimental data.

claim: Tet3 does not recruit MeCP2 or may even repel it.
source: Since MeCP2 tBDNF binding is reduced when Tet1 is replaced by Tet3, it is tempting to speculate that Tet3 does not recruit MeCP2 or may even repel it.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed binding patterns.

claim: DNA binding by CTCF is repelled by the presence of 5mC while it preferentially binds to unmethylated C or possibly oxidized derivatives of 5mC.
source: DNA binding by CTCF is repelled by the presence of 5mC while, in contrast, it preferentially binds to unmethylated C or possibly oxidized derivatives of 5mC (Shukla et al., 2011; Spruijt et al., 2013; Marina et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CTCF colocalizes to DNA domains enriched in active histone marks such as H3K4me3 or H3K36me3 and is generally excluded from regions with elevated repressive marks including H3K27me3 or H3K9me3.
source: Additionally, CTCF colocalizes to DNA domains enriched in active histone marks such as H3K4me3 or H3K36me3 and is generally excluded from regions with elevated repressive marks including H3K27me3 or H3K9me3 (Saldaña-Meyer and Recillas-Targa, 2011; Ali et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Significantly elevated ChIP for CTCF was observed in two regions of the tBDNF coding sequence after classical conditioning surveyed by primer sets P1 proximally and P3 located more distally.
source: We observed significantly elevated ChIP for CTCF in two regions of the tBDNF coding sequence after classical conditioning surveyed by primer sets P1 proximally and P3 located more distally (and within the splice site).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data.

claim: Enhanced CTCF binding was associated with DNA demethylation and a reduction in 5hmC.
source: This enhanced binding was associated with DNA demethylation and a reduction in 5hmC.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined ChIP, BSP, and MeDIP data.

claim: Shukla et al. (2011) provided evidence that CD45 exon inclusion was related to CTCF binding and RNAPII pausing.
source: Shukla et al. (2011) provided evidence that CD45 exon inclusion was related to CTCF binding and RNAPII pausing.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Decreased ChIP for RNAPIISer2 and slower rates of transcription corresponded with increased presence of CTCF which was thought to act as a physical barrier to RNAPII and allow more time for splice site recognition.
source: They showed that decreased ChIP for RNAPIISer2 and slower rates of transcription corresponded with increased presence of CTCF which was thought to act as a physical barrier to RNAPII and allow more time for splice site recognition (Luco et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CTCF may have dual functions in regulating alternative splicing, through RNAPII pausing to promote it or by its insulator function to inhibit it.
source: It is possible that CTCF has dual functions in regulating alternative splicing, through RNAPII pausing to promote it or by its insulator function to inhibit it.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the current findings and previous literature.

claim: CTCF along with binding partner cohesin are involved in chromatin looping that bends DNA located between paired binding sites of CTCF/cohesin.
source: CTCF along with binding partner cohesin are also involved in chromatin looping that bends DNA located between paired binding sites of CTCF/cohesin (Ali et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Two regions in the tBDNF coding sequence showed significantly elevated CTCF binding after conditioning, a proximal region (P1) and a distal region (P3) located within the splice site itself.
source: In consideration of the chromatin looping model, it is intriguing that two regions in the tBDNF coding sequence were observed to show significantly elevated CTCF binding after conditioning, a proximal region (P1) in which MeCP2-YB-1 binding/dissociation is correlated with splicing and a distal region (P3) located within the splice site itself.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data.

claim: The two CTCF binding sites may reflect paired CTCF/cohesin interactions required for loop formation that protects the tBDNF splice site from splicing.
source: These may reflect paired CTCF/cohesin interactions required for loop formation that protects the tBDNF splice site from splicing.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed binding pattern and chromatin looping models.

claim: There are only 374 bp separating the P1 and P3 CTCF binding sites in the coding sequence.
source: However, there are only 374 bp separating the P1 and P3 CTCF binding sites in the coding sequence and it is uncertain how short DNA loops occurring in nature can be or if short-range loops might be mediated by CTCF/cohesin.
evidence: This is based on the known sequence and primer locations.

claim: It is uncertain how short DNA loops occurring in nature can be or if short-range loops might be mediated by CTCF/cohesin.

claim: Aberrant pre-mRNA alternative splicing is thought to be an important factor in generating the suite of abnormalities observed in patients with the neurodevelopmental disorder RTT.
source: Aberrant pre-mRNA alternative splicing is thought to be an important factor in generating the suite of abnormalities observed in patients with the neurodevelopmental disorder RTT and implicates MeCP2 in splicing mechanisms (Young et al., 2005; Bienvenu and Chelly, 2006; Maunakea et al., 2013; Li et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MeCP2 was reported to interact with YB-1 and Prpf3.
